The second: It is one of the names of the Qur'an. This is said by Qatadah.

The third: It is one of the names of God Most High, by which He swore. This is said by Ibn Abbas.

The fourth: It is a letter of the alphabet (harf hijaʾ) that is one of the names of God Most High. This is said by al-Suddi.

The fifth: It means "God has spoken truly" (sadaqa Allah). This is said by al-Dahhak.

The sixth: It derives from al-musadda (opposition), which is confrontation, and its meaning is: "Confront the Qur'an with your knowledge." This is said by al-Hasan.

The seventh: It derives from al-musadda (opposition), which is following, and its meaning is: "Follow the Qur'an with your knowledge." This is said by Sufyan.

﴿By the Qur'an, full of reminder﴾. On this there are four interpretations:

The first: "Full of honour." This is said by Ibn Abbas, Said ibn Jubayr and al-Suddi.

The second: "With clarification." This is said by Qatadah.

The third: "With admonition." This is said by al-Dahhak.

The fourth: "Mention of what came before it of the scriptures." This is related by Ibn Qutaybah.

Qatadah said: "Here the oath occurs."

(p-٧٦)The interpreters differed concerning its answer (jawab) on two views:

One of them: The answer of the oath is omitted, and omitting it is more magnificent for it, because the soul goes in every direction in it.

Those who said it is omitted differed on it on two views:

One of them: The omitted part is estimated as "Indeed the Truth has come."

The second: Its estimate is "The matter is not as they say."

The second view: From the origin, the answer of the oath is expressed. Those who said it is expressed differed on it on two views:

One of them: The saying of God Most High: ﴿How many generations did We destroy before them﴾. This is said by al-Farra'.

The second: From the saying of God Most High: ﴿Indeed that is true: the disputing of the people of the Fire﴾. This is the view of Muqatil.

His saying, Exalted and Mighty is He: ﴿But those who disbelieve are in arrogance and opposition﴾. On this there are three aspects:

The first: That is, in zeal and separation. This is said by Qatadah.

The second: In self-exaltation and disagreement. This is said by al-Suddi.

The third: In disdain and enmity.

It may also admit a fourth: In refusal and keeping away.

﴿How many did We destroy before them﴾: that is, before the disbelievers of this community.

﴿of generations﴾ (qarn). On this there are two views:

One of them: That is, of nations. This is said by Abu Malik.

The second: That the qarn is a measured period of time, and on it there are seven sayings:

The first: It is twenty years. This is said by al-Hasan.

The second: Forty years. This is said by Ibrahim.

The third: Sixty years. Narrated by Abu Ubayda al-Naji.

The fourth: Seventy years. This is said by Qatadah.

The fifth: Eighty years. This is said by al-Kalbi.

The sixth: One hundred years. Narrated by Abdullah ibn Bishr from the Prophet (ﷺ).

(p-٧٧)The seventh: One hundred and twenty years. This is said by Zurarah ibn Awfa.

His saying, Exalted and Mighty is He: ﴿Then they cried out, but it was no time for escape﴾. It admits two aspects:

One of them: They sought help.

The second: They called out.

﴿but it was no time for escape (mans)﴾. The taʾ of lā (lāt) is separated from the ḥāʾ of ḥīn, and it is written so in the Mushaf. Whoever joins it to the ḥāʾ has erred.

On it there are two aspects:

One of them: It means "not" (lā). This is the view of Abu Ubayda.

The second: It means "not" in the sense of laysa (is not), and it governs only the noun ḥīn (time) specifically. The poet said:

"You remember the love of Layla, when it is no longer time (lāt ḥīnan), and grey hair has come and cut off the companion."

On the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and it was no time for escape﴾ there are five aspects:

The first: "And it was not a time of refuge." This is said by Zayd ibn Aslam.

The second: "And it was not a time of rescue." Narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn Abbas. From this is the saying of Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, in his rajaz:

"I shall surely strike the disobedient son of the disobedient, with seventy thousand, binding their forelocks, who have turned the horses aside from the coats of mail, lions of the thicket, when there is no escape."

The third: "And it was not a time of cessation." Narrated by Abu Qabus from Ibn Abbas. From this is the saying of the poet:

"So they are humbled for blood-money, with no escape for them, gathered by an assembly that heals from the hunt."

The fourth: "And it was not a time of fleeing." This is said by Ikrimah, al-Dahhak and Qatadah. Al-Farra' said: it is a verbal noun from nasa yanusu.

Al-nawṣ with the nūn is to fall back, and al-bawṣ with the bāʾ is to advance. He recited the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"Because of the remembrance of Layla, if she turns you away, you retreat, falling short of her by a step, and you advance (tabūṣ)."

(p-٧٨)In this verse he combined al-bawṣ and al-nawṣ, so with the nūn it means to fall back, and with the bāʾ it means to advance.

The fifth: That al-nawṣ with the nūn means advancing, and al-bawṣ with the bāʾ means falling back, and it is one of the words with opposite meanings (min al-adad). When they sensed a failure in battle, some of them would say to others: "Manas!", meaning one single charge, in which whoever is saved is saved and whoever perishes perishes. This is narrated by al-Kalbi. Thus its interpretation on this aspect becomes what al-Suddi said: that when they saw death, they could find no escape from the punishment, nor a return to repentance.

**Verse 4–11**

His Exalted and Majestic words: ﴿Has he made the gods into one God? Indeed, this is a strange thing!﴾ He commanded them to say: "There is no god but Allah." Could one God suffice for all our needs? "Indeed, this is a strange thing" (ʿujāb) in the sense of ʿajīb (strange), as one says rajulun ṭuwālun and ṭawīlun (a tall man). Al-Khalil (Ibn Ahmad al-Farahidi) distinguished between them in meaning, saying: "al-ʿajīb is that of which there may be a like, while al-ʿujāb is that of which there is no like." The same applies to ṭawīl and ṭuwāl.

His Exalted and Majestic words: ﴿And the chiefs among them went away﴾. al-Inṭilāq means going away with ease, and from it comes ṭalāqat al-wajh (cheerfulness of the face). Regarding "the chiefs among them" there are two views:

First: he is ʿUqbah ibn Muʿayṭ, as said by Mujahid.

Second: he is Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, who came to Abu Talib during his illness, complaining about the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), then went away from him when he despaired of his being swayed. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

﴿Walk on and persevere for your gods﴾. In this there are two meanings:

(p-79) First: leave him and worship your gods.

Second: persist in your opposition and persevere in your worship of your gods. The Arabs say: "Walk on this matter," meaning: proceed with it and hold fast to it.

﴿Indeed, this is a thing that is intended﴾. In this there are two meanings:

First: when ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) embraced Islam and Islam was strengthened by him, it grieved the Quraysh, and they said: "The conversion of ʿUmar is a strengthening of Islam, and it is a thing that is intended." This was said by Muqatil.

Second: Muhammad's opposition to us and his separation from our religion are only intended by him for leadership over us and dominion over us.

His Exalted and Majestic words: ﴿We have not heard of this in the latest religion﴾. In this there are four sayings:

First: it refers to Christianity, because it was the last of the religions. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatadah and al-Suddi.

Second: it refers to the period between ʿIsa and Muhammad (peace be upon them both). This was said by al-Hakam.

Third: it refers to the religion of the Quraysh. This was said by Mujahid.

Fourth: its meaning is that we have not heard that this would occur in our time. This was said by al-Hasan.

﴿This is nothing but a fabrication﴾, that is, a lie that Muhammad (ﷺ) invented.

His Exalted and Majestic words: ﴿Or do they have the treasuries of the mercy of your Lord?﴾ al-Suddi said: the keys of prophethood, so that they give it to whomever they wish and withhold it from whomever they wish.

His Exalted and Majestic words: ﴿Then let them ascend by the means﴾. In this there are four interpretations:

First: into the heaven. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Second: into merit and religion. This was said by al-Suddi.

Third: by the paths of the heaven and its gates. This was said by Mujahid.

Fourth: its meaning is: let them rise high by the means of power, if they think that these are preventive. This is the meaning of the statement of Abu ʿUbaydah.

(p-80) His Exalted and Majestic words: ﴿A host of the factions, routed there﴾. Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: they are the polytheists of Makkah. The word ﴿mā﴾ here is a ṣilah (a supplementary particle for emphasis). You say: "I came to you for a certain matter (li-amrin mā)."

Al-Aʿsha said:

"Go away, as far as you are concerned; forbearance has overtaken me, and my occupations have kept me from your agitation."

The meaning of His words "a host" (jund) is: followers who imitate, among whom there is no knowledgeable guide.

﴿Routed from the factions﴾ means the polytheists of Quraysh, who are the factions of Iblis and his followers. It was also said that they are called factions because they banded together in denial of Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ). Qatadah said: He gave him the good news of their defeat while he was in Makkah, and its fulfilment was on the Day of Badr.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 38, verses 12–16:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The people of Noah denied before them﴾. God, exalted and majestic, mentioned the people with a feminine form of expression. The grammarians (ahl al-'Arabiyya) differed regarding its feminine form on two views. The first: it is permissible to use both the feminine and the masculine with it. The second: its wording is masculine and it is not permissible to make it feminine, except when the meaning refers to a clan (ashira), so the implied meaning's rule is given precedence in the wording as an alert to it, like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Nay, indeed it is a reminder﴾ and ﴿so whoever wills may take heed of it﴾, and He did not say "dhakarahā," because the implied element in it had been mentioned, so He made it masculine even though the wording required the feminine.

﴿And 'Ad﴾, and they are the people of Hud. They lived in al-Ahqaf, in the land of Yemen. Ibn Ishaq said: They were worshippers of idols, which were three: one of them was called Hadar, another Samur, and another al-Hana. Hud commanded them to affirm the oneness of God, glorified is He, and not to set up any god alongside Him, and to refrain from wronging people; he did not command them except with this.

﴿And Pharaoh, master of the stakes﴾. Regarding his being called master of the stakes, there are four sayings:

The first: he had many buildings, and buildings are called stakes; this was said by al-Dahhak.

The second: he had playgrounds of stakes on which he would play; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada.

The third: because he would torment people with stakes; this was said by al-Suddi.

The fourth: it means one whose kingship is firm and whose strength is great, like the firmness of what is fixed with stakes, as al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur said:

"They lived therein in the most pleasant of lives, in the shade of a kingdom whose stakes were firm."

﴿And Thamud﴾, and they are Arabs. Muqatil related that 'Ad and Thamud were cousins. The dwellings of Thamud were in al-Hijr, between the Hijaz and al-Sham, among them the Wadi al-Qura. God sent Salih to them, and it is disputed regarding their faith in him. Ibn 'Abbas mentioned that they believed, then he died, and they reverted from faith after him; so God revived him, sent him to them, and informed them that he was Salih. They denied him and said: "Salih has died; so bring us what you promise us, if you are of the truthful." Then God sent them the she-camel; they disbelieved and hamstrung her, so God destroyed them.

Ibn Ishaq said: God sent Salih as a young man, and he called them until he became an old man; they hamstrung the she-camel and did not believe until they perished.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they say: Our Lord, hasten for us our share (qitt)﴾, to the end of the verse.

Concerning it there are five interpretations:

The first: the meaning is, hasten for us our portion of the Garden which You promised us; said by Ibn Jubayr.

The second: hasten for us our portion of the punishment which You promised us, mocking it; said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: hasten for us our provision; said by Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid.

The fourth: show us our dwellings; said by al-Suddi.

The fifth: hasten for us in this world our book (record) that is in the Hereafter, and this is His saying, ﴿As for him who is given his book in his right hand﴾ and ﴿As for him who is given his book in his left hand﴾, mocking it.

The original root of qitt is cutting, and from it comes "qatta al-qalam" (he cut the pen), and the saying "ma ra'aytuhu qatt" (I have not seen him ever), meaning time has cut between me and him. It is applied to a portion, (p-83) to a book, and to provision, because it is cut off from others; however, in the sense of a book it is more commonly used and more literal. Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said:

For whoever holds this view there are two sayings:

The first: it applies to every document by which one is secured.

The second: it is specific to a document in which there is a gift and a bond, said by Ibn Bahr.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Be patient over what they say﴾, meaning: as the steadfast messengers (ulu al-'azm) were patient, not like the one who was not patient, such as Jonah (Yunus).

The fourth: knowledge and understanding. This was said by Shurayh.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 38, verses 21–25:**

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Has the news of the disputants reached you?﴾ The word *khasm* (disputant) applies to one, two, and a group, because its origin is the verbal noun (*masdar*).

﴿When they climbed over the walls of the prayer niche.﴾ The meaning of *tasawwaru* is that they came to him from above a wall. Regarding *al-mihrab* (the prayer niche) there are four opinions:

The first: it is the front of the assembly, and from it comes the *mihrab* of the mosque. This was said by Abu 'Ubayda.

The second: it is the assembly of the nobles, over which people contend because of the honor of its owner. This was related by Ibn 'Isa.

The third: it is the mosque. This was said by Yahya ibn Salam.

The fourth: it is the upper chamber, because they climbed over the wall to reach him in it.

﴿When they entered upon Dawud and he was startled by them.﴾ The reason for this, as related by Ibn 'Isa, is that Dawud (peace be upon him) said to himself: "If I am tested, I will guard myself." It was said to him: "You will indeed be tested, and you will know the day on which you are tested, so take your precaution." He took the *Zabur* (Psalms) and entered the *mihrab*, and he forbade anyone from entering upon him. While he was reading the *Zabur*, a bird came, the most beautiful of birds, and began hopping before him. He intended to catch it with his hand, and it lured him on until it fell into a window of the *mihrab*. He approached it to take it, but it fluttered away, so he looked up to see it, and he gazed upon a woman who was bathing. When she saw him, she covered her body with her hair. Al-Suddi said: "She fell into his heart." Ibn 'Abbas said: "Her husband was a warrior in the way of Allah." Muqatil said: "He was Uriya ibn Hanan. Dawud wrote to the commander of the army that he should place her husband in the vanguard of the carriers of the *tabut* (the Ark). The carriers of the *tabut* were either granted victory by Allah or killed. So he sent him forward among them, and he was killed. When her waiting period ended, Dawud proposed to her, and she stipulated that if she bore a boy he would be the caliph after him. She wrote a document to this effect and called fifty men of the Children of Israel as witnesses against him. He did not perceive her trial until she bore Sulayman, who grew up. Then the two angels climbed over him, and what took place between them is what Allah related in His Book."

Regarding his fright at them, there are two opinions:

The first: because they climbed over the wall to reach him without a door.

The second: because they came to him at a time other than his time for sitting in judgment.

﴿They said: "Do not fear. Two disputants, one of us has wronged the other."﴾ They were two angels, and they were neither disputants nor wrongdoers, and no falsehood proceeds from them. The sense of their speech is: "What would you say if two disputants came to you and said: one of us has wronged the other?"

He used the dual here, and the plural in the first verse, when He said: ﴿Has the news of the disputants reached you?﴾ because their whole group is gathered together, and they are two parties, each one of which is a disputant.

﴿So judge between us with truth﴾ i.e., with justice.

﴿And do not deviate﴾ Regarding this there are three interpretations:

The first: do not be partial. This was said by Qatada.

The second: do not be unjust. This was said by al-Suddi.

The third: do not be excessive. This was said by al-Akhfash.

Regarding the origin of *shatat* (deviation), there are two opinions:

The first: its origin is distance, from the saying "the house became distant (*shatat al-dar*) when it went far." The poet said:

Tushtitu ghadan dar jiranina wa-l-dar ba'da ghadin abʿadu
(Tomorrow our neighbors' house will be far, and the house after tomorrow will be farther.)

The second: it means excess.

The poet said:

Ala ya li-qawmi qad ishatta 'awadhili * wa-za'amna an awda bi-haqqi batiluhi
(Oh my people, my blamers have gone to excess, and they claim that my falsehood has ruined my right.)

﴿And guide us to the even path.﴾ Regarding this there are two meanings:

The first: guide us to the aim of truth. This was said by Yahya.

The second: to the justice of judgment. This was said by al-Suddi.

﴿Indeed, this is my brother.﴾ Regarding this there are two meanings:

The first: he means in my religion. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud.

The second: he means my companion. This was said by al-Suddi.

﴿He has ninety-nine ewes and I have one ewe.﴾ Regarding this there are two meanings:

The first: he meant ninety-nine women, and he referred to them metaphorically as ewes. This was said by Ibn 'Isa.

Qutrub said: "The *na'jah* (ewe) is the beautiful, soft woman."

The second: he meant the ewes, to give Dawud an example. This was said by al-Hasan.

﴿So he said: "Give her to me to be in my charge."﴾ Regarding this there are three meanings:

The first: include her with me. This was said by Yahya.

The second: give her to me. This was said by al-Hasan.

The third: move over from her to me. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud.

﴿And he overpowered me in speech.﴾ Regarding this there are three opinions:

The first: he overpowered me in the dispute. This was said by Qatada.

The second: he overcame me regarding my right, from the saying "whoever is mighty (*'aziz*) plunders," i.e., whoever overcomes, seizes. This was said by Ibn 'Isa.

The third: its meaning is: if he speaks, he is more eloquent; if he strikes, he is stronger than me; if he calls out, he is louder than me. This was said by al-Dahhak.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿He said: "He has certainly wronged you by demanding your ewe in addition to his ewes."﴾ If it is asked, how can he judge for one of the two disputants against the other on the basis of his claim? There are two answers to this:

The first: the other had already acknowledged this, so Dawud (peace be upon him) judged against him on the basis of his acknowledgment, and it was omitted, relying on the listener's understanding. This was said by al-Suddi.

The second: if the matter is as you say, then "he has certainly wronged you by demanding your ewe in addition to his ewes."

﴿And indeed, many of the associates﴾ may have two meanings:

The first: companions.

The second: partners.

﴿Oppress one another﴾ i.e., transgress.

﴿Except those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ its implied sense: "they do not oppress one another," and this was omitted, relying on the listener's understanding.

﴿And few are they﴾ Regarding this there are two meanings:

The first: "and few are those among them who oppress one another." This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: "and few are those who do not oppress one another." This was said by Qatada.

Regarding the *ma* in His saying ﴿and few are they﴾ there are two opinions:

The first: it is an extra, superfluous particle; its sense is: "and few are they."

The second: it means *alladhi* (who); its sense is: "and few are those who are like that."

﴿And Dawud thought that We had only tested him.﴾ Qatada said: i.e., Dawud knew that We had only tested him. Regarding this there are three meanings:

The first: We tried him. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: We afflicted him. This was said by al-Suddi.

The third: We made the worship harder upon him. This was said by Ibn 'Isa.

﴿So he sought forgiveness from his Lord﴾ for his sin.

Qatada said: The Prophet of Allah (peace be upon him) passed judgment against himself without noticing it. When the sin became clear to him, he sought forgiveness from his Lord.

Regarding the sin there are four opinions:

The first: he heard from one of the two disputants and ruled in his favor before hearing from the other.

The second: his eye fell upon the wife of Uriya ibn Hanan, whose name was Yasha', while she was bathing, and he gazed at her to his fill until she became fixed in his heart.

The third: it was what he intended, that if her husband were killed he would marry her and treat her well as a wife. This was said by al-Hasan.

Al-Suddi related from 'Ali (may Allah honor his face) that he said: "If I heard a man mention that Dawud had committed a forbidden act with that woman, I would flog him one hundred and sixty times, because the legal punishment for ordinary people is eighty, and the legal punishment for prophets is one hundred and sixty, two punishments."

﴿And he fell down bowing and turned in repentance.﴾ i.e., he fell down prostrating. Prostration is sometimes expressed by the word *ruku'* (bowing). The poet said:

Fakharra 'ala wajhihi rakiʿan * wa-taba ila-llahi min kulli dhanbin
(He fell upon his face, bowing, and turned to Allah from every sin.)

Mujahid said: He remained prostrate for forty days, not lifting his head, until plants grew from the tears of his eyes, so he covered his head. Then Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿So We forgave him that, and indeed for him with Us is a near station and a good return.﴾ i.e., a place of return.

Regarding *zulfa* (near station) there are two meanings:

The first: honor, and this is the well-known view.

The second: mercy. This was said by al-Dahhak.

So he raised his head, and his forehead had been wounded.

Regarding this prostration there are two opinions:

The first: it is a *sajdat 'azima* (prostration of obligation, a prostration required upon recitation of its verse), which is performed when reciting it in prayer and outside prayer. This was said by Abu Hanifa.

The second: it is a *sajdat shukr* (prostration of thankfulness), which is not performed upon recitation of it, neither in prayer nor outside prayer. This is the view of al-Shafi'i.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Dawud remained for a while not drinking water without mixing it with his tears, not eating food without moistening it with his tears, and not sleeping on a bed without soaking it with his tears.

It is related of Dawud that he used to supplicate against sinners, but when he committed the sin he would not pass by a valley without saying: "O Allah, forgive the sinners, perhaps You will forgive me along with them."

She wrote a document to this effect and called fifty men of the Children of Israel as witnesses against him. He did not perceive her trial until she bore Sulayman, who grew up. Then the two angels climbed over him, and what took place between them is what Allah related in His Book."

Regarding his fright at them, there are two opinions:

The first: because they climbed over the wall to reach him without a door.

The second: because they came to him at a time other than his time for sitting in judgment.

﴿They said: "Do not fear. Two disputants, one of us has wronged the other."﴾ They were two angels, and they were neither disputants nor wrongdoers, and no falsehood proceeds from them. The sense of their speech is: "What would you say if two disputants came to you and said: one of us has wronged the other?"

He used the dual here, and the plural in the first verse, when He said: ﴿Has the news of the disputants reached you?﴾ because their whole group is gathered together, and they are two parties, each one of which is a disputant.

﴿So judge between us with truth﴾ i.e., with justice.

﴿And do not deviate﴾ Regarding this there are three interpretations:

The first: do not be partial. This was said by Qatada.

The second: do not be unjust. This was said by al-Suddi.

The third: do not be excessive. This was said by al-Akhfash.

Regarding the origin of *shatat* (deviation), there are two opinions:

The first: its origin is distance, from the saying "the house became distant (*shatat al-dar*) when it went far." The poet said:

Tushtitu ghadan dar jiranina wa-l-dar ba'da ghadin abʿadu
(Tomorrow our neighbors' house will be far, and the house after tomorrow will be farther.)

The second: it means excess.

The poet said:

Ala ya li-qawmi qad ishatta 'awadhili * wa-za'amna an awda bi-haqqi batiluhi
(Oh my people, my blamers have gone to excess, and they claim that my falsehood has ruined my right.)

﴿And guide us to the even path.﴾ Regarding this there are two meanings:

The first: guide us to the aim of truth. This was said by Yahya.

The second: to the justice of judgment. This was said by al-Suddi.

﴿Indeed, this is my brother.﴾ Regarding this there are two meanings:

The first: he means in my religion. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud.

The second: he means my companion. This was said by al-Suddi.

﴿He has ninety-nine ewes and I have one ewe.﴾ Regarding this there are two meanings:

The first: he meant ninety-nine women, and he referred to them metaphorically as ewes. This was said by Ibn 'Isa.

Qutrub said: "The *na'jah* (ewe) is the beautiful, soft woman."

The second: he meant the ewes, to give Dawud an example. This was said by al-Hasan.

﴿So he said: "Give her to me to be in my charge."﴾ Regarding this there are three meanings:

The first: include her with me. This was said by Yahya.

The second: give her to me. This was said by al-Hasan.

The third: move over from her to me. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud.

﴿And he overpowered me in speech.﴾ Regarding this there are three opinions:

The first: he overpowered me in the dispute. This was said by Qatada.

The second: he overcame me regarding my right, from the saying "whoever is mighty (*'aziz*) plunders," i.e., whoever overcomes, seizes. This was said by Ibn 'Isa.

The third: its meaning is: if he speaks, he is more eloquent; if he strikes, he is stronger than me; if he calls out, he is louder than me. This was said by al-Dahhak.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿He said: "He has certainly wronged you by demanding your ewe in addition to his ewes."﴾ If it is asked, how can he judge for one of the two disputants against the other on the basis of his claim? There are two answers to this:

The first: the other had already acknowledged this, so Dawud (peace be upon him) judged against him on the basis of his acknowledgment, and it was omitted, relying on the listener's understanding. This was said by al-Suddi.

The second: if the matter is as you say, then "he has certainly wronged you by demanding your ewe in addition to his ewes."

﴿And indeed, many of the associates﴾ may have two meanings:

The first: companions.

The second: partners.

﴿Oppress one another﴾ i.e., transgress.

﴿Except those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ its implied sense: "they do not oppress one another," and this was omitted, relying on the listener's understanding.

﴿And few are they﴾ Regarding this there are two meanings:

The first: "and few are those among them who oppress one another." This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: "and few are those who do not oppress one another." This was said by Qatada.

Regarding the *ma* in His saying ﴿and few are they﴾ there are two opinions:

The first: it is an extra, superfluous particle; its sense is: "and few are they."

The second: it means *alladhi* (who); its sense is: "and few are those who are like that."

﴿And Dawud thought that We had only tested him.﴾ Qatada said: i.e., Dawud knew that We had only tested him. Regarding this there are three meanings:

The first: We tried him. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: We afflicted him. This was said by al-Suddi.

The third: We made the worship harder upon him. This was said by Ibn 'Isa.

﴿So he sought forgiveness from his Lord﴾ for his sin.

Qatada said: The Prophet of Allah (peace be upon him) passed judgment against himself without noticing it. When the sin became clear to him, he sought forgiveness from his Lord.

Regarding the sin there are four opinions:

The first: he heard from one of the two disputants and ruled in his favor before hearing from the other.

The second: his eye fell upon the wife of Uriya ibn Hanan, whose name was Yasha', while she was bathing, and he gazed at her to his fill until she became fixed in his heart.

The third: it was what he intended, that if her husband were killed he would marry her and treat her well as a wife. This was said by al-Hasan.

Al-Suddi related from 'Ali (may Allah honor his face) that he said: "If I heard a man mention that Dawud had committed a forbidden act with that woman, I would flog him one hundred and sixty times, because the legal punishment for ordinary people is eighty, and the legal punishment for prophets is one hundred and sixty, two punishments."

﴿And he fell down bowing and turned in repentance.﴾ i.e., he fell down prostrating. Prostration is sometimes expressed by the word *ruku'* (bowing). The poet said:

Fakharra 'ala wajhihi rakiʿan * wa-taba ila-llahi min kulli dhanbin
(He fell upon his face, bowing, and turned to Allah from every sin.)

Mujahid said: He remained prostrate for forty days, not lifting his head, until plants grew from the tears of his eyes, so he covered his head. Then Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿So We forgave him that, and indeed for him with Us is a near station and a good return.﴾ i.e., a place of return.

Regarding *zulfa* (near station) there are two meanings:

The first: honor, and this is the well-known view.

The second: mercy. This was said by al-Dahhak.

So he raised his head, and his forehead had been wounded.

Regarding this prostration there are two opinions:

The first: it is a *sajdat 'azima* (prostration of obligation, a prostration required upon recitation of its verse), which is performed when reciting it in prayer and outside prayer. This was said by Abu Hanifa.

The second: it is a *sajdat shukr* (prostration of thankfulness), which is not performed upon recitation of it, neither in prayer nor outside prayer. This is the view of al-Shafi'i.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Dawud remained for a while not drinking water without mixing it with his tears, not eating food without moistening it with his tears, and not sleeping on a bed without soaking it with his tears.

It is related of Dawud that he used to supplicate against sinners, but when he committed the sin he would not pass by a valley without saying: "O Allah, forgive the sinners, perhaps You will forgive me along with them."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 38, verse 26:

One of them: a khalifah (vicegerent) of God, Exalted is He, and the khilafah (caliphate) here is prophethood.

The second: a khalifah of those who came before you, because the one who remains is the successor of the one who passed away, and the khilafah here is kingship (al-mulk).

﴿So judge between the people with truth﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations:

One of them: with justice.

The second: with the truth that is binding upon you toward us.

﴿And do not follow desire﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations:

One of them: that you incline toward the one you desire and so act unjustly.

The second: that you judge according to what you desire and so slip.

(p-91) ﴿For it will lead you astray from the way of God﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations:

One of them: from the religion of God.

The second: from the obedience of God.

﴿Indeed, those who go astray from the way of God will have a severe punishment for having forgotten the Day of Reckoning﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations:

One of them: for having abandoned action for the Day of Reckoning; this was said by al-Suddi.

The second: for having turned away from the Day of Reckoning; this was said by al-Hasan.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 38, verses 27–33:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿When there were displayed before him, at evening, the poised, swift steeds﴾. "The horses" (al-khayl). In this there are two interpretations:

The first: their "sufun" (ṣufūn, poised stance) is their standing. From this is what is related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Whoever would like men to stand before him in ranks, let him take his seat in the Fire." That is, they keep standing for him continuously. Qutrub related this, and he recited the verse of al-Nabigha:

"For us is a tent pitched in its courtyard, noble she-camels of the best breed and the swift, poised horses."

(p-92) The second: their "sufun" is raising one of their forelegs at the tip of the hoof until they stand on three legs, as the poet said:

"He has accustomed the poised stance, and it never ceases, as if it, of what stands on three legs, is lame."

Regarding ﴿al-jiyad﴾ (the swift, fine steeds) there are two interpretations:

The first: they are those with long necks, derived from "al-jid," which is the neck, because the length of horses' necks is one of the qualities of their nobility.

The second: they are the swift ones. This was said by Mujahid. Its singular is "jawad," so named because it "yajud" (gives generously) with its running.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿So he said, "Indeed, I have loved the love of good"﴾. In this there are three interpretations:

The first: it means the love of wealth. This was said by Ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak.

The second: the love of horses. This was said by Qatada and al-Suddi.

From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Good is tied to the forelocks of horses until the Day of Resurrection." In the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud: "the love of horses."

The third: the love of this world. This was said by Asbat.

Regarding ﴿I have loved the love of good﴾ there are two interpretations:

The first: there is inversion in it. Its estimated form is: "I loved good with love," and then it was placed first, so he said: "I loved the love of good," then he made it an annexed construction and said "uhibbu al-khayr." This was said by some grammarians.

The second: the speech follows its arrangement without any inversion or transposition, and its interpretation is: "I preferred the love of good."

﴿from the remembrance of my Lord﴾. In this there are two interpretations:

The first: from the afternoon prayer (ṣalat al-'aṣr). This was said by 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him.

The second: from the remembrance of Allah, exalted is He. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

(p-93) Al-Harith related from 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked about the middle prayer (al-salat al-wusta) and he said: 'It is the afternoon prayer, which the Prophet of Allah Sulayman, peace be upon him, neglected.'"

﴿until it was hidden behind the veil﴾. In this there are two views:

The first: until the sun was hidden behind the veil, and the veil is a green mountain encircling creation. This was said by Qatada and Ka'b.

The second: the horses were hidden behind the veil, i.e., he was occupied with the remembrance of his Lord up to that state. This was related by Ibn 'Isa.

The veil is also the night, called a veil because it conceals what is in it.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿"Bring them back to me"﴾, meaning the horses, because they were displayed before him and were running in front of him, and nothing of them could be discerned due to their speed, while he was saying: "O Allah, I have lowered my gaze," until they disappeared behind the veil. Then he said: "Bring them back to me."

﴿So he began passing his hand over the shanks and necks﴾. In this there are two views:

The first: out of his intense love for them, he passed his hand over their hocks and necks. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: when he saw that they had distracted him from the prayer, he struck their hocks and necks. This was said by al-Hasan and Qatada.

(p-94) What he was distracted from of the prayer was not an obligatory prayer, but a voluntary one, because abandoning an obligation deliberately is wickedness, and he did that as a discipline for himself.

Horses are permissible to eat, so that was not for him a destruction for which he would be sinful.

Al-Kalbi said: They were a thousand horses, and he hamstrung nine hundred, and a hundred remained from them.

Therefore, what is in the hands of people of the noble horses is from the offspring of that hundred.

Regarding ﴿al-jiyad﴾ (the swift, fine steeds) there are two interpretations:

The first: they are those with long necks, derived from "al-jid," which is the neck, because the length of horses' necks is one of the qualities of their nobility.

The second: they are the swift ones. This was said by Mujahid. Its singular is "jawad," so named because it "yajud" (gives generously) with its running.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿So he said, "Indeed, I have loved the love of good"﴾. In this there are three interpretations:

The first: it means the love of wealth. This was said by Ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak.

The second: the love of horses. This was said by Qatada and al-Suddi.

From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Good is tied to the forelocks of horses until the Day of Resurrection." In the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud: "the love of horses."

The third: the love of this world. This was said by Asbat.

Regarding ﴿I have loved the love of good﴾ there are two interpretations:

The first: there is inversion in it. Its estimated form is: "I loved good with love," and then it was placed first, so he said: "I loved the love of good," then he made it an annexed construction and said "uhibbu al-khayr." This was said by some grammarians.

The second: the speech follows its arrangement without any inversion or transposition, and its interpretation is: "I preferred the love of good."

﴿from the remembrance of my Lord﴾. In this there are two interpretations:

The first: from the afternoon prayer (ṣalat al-'aṣr). This was said by 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him.

The second: from the remembrance of Allah, exalted is He. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

(p-93) Al-Harith related from 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked about the middle prayer (al-salat al-wusta) and he said: 'It is the afternoon prayer, which the Prophet of Allah Sulayman, peace be upon him, neglected.'"

﴿until it was hidden behind the veil﴾. In this there are two views:

The first: until the sun was hidden behind the veil, and the veil is a green mountain encircling creation. This was said by Qatada and Ka'b.

The second: the horses were hidden behind the veil, i.e., he was occupied with the remembrance of his Lord up to that state. This was related by Ibn 'Isa.

The veil is also the night, called a veil because it conceals what is in it.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿"Bring them back to me"﴾, meaning the horses, because they were displayed before him and were running in front of him, and nothing of them could be discerned due to their speed, while he was saying: "O Allah, I have lowered my gaze," until they disappeared behind the veil. Then he said: "Bring them back to me."

﴿So he began passing his hand over the shanks and necks﴾. In this there are two views:

The first: out of his intense love for them, he passed his hand over their hocks and necks. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: when he saw that they had distracted him from the prayer, he struck their hocks and necks. This was said by al-Hasan and Qatada.

Therefore, what is in the hands of people of the noble horses is from the offspring of that hundred.

﴿And We certainly tested Solomon﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations:

First: it means We tried him. This is related by al-Suddi.

Second: We punished him. This is related by al-Naqqash.

Concerning the trial by which he was punished, there are six opinions:

First: he approached some of his wives during menstruation or something else. This is related by al-Hasan.

Second: what Ibn 'Abbas related: he said, Solomon had a woman called Jarada. Her family had a dispute with a people, and they brought the matter before Solomon. He judged between them with the truth, but he wished that the right had been with her family. It was then said to him, "Affliction will befall you," and he kept wondering whether the affliction would come to him from the earth or from the sky.

Third: what Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib related: Solomon secluded himself from the people for three days, not judging between anyone and not granting justice to the wronged against the wrongdoer. So God Most High revealed to him: "I did not appoint you so that you would be hidden from My servants, but so that you would judge between them and grant justice to their wronged."

Fourth: what Shahr ibn Hawshab related: Solomon took captive the daughter of the king of Ghazzan on an island of the islands of the sea called Saydun. Love for her was cast upon him, while she turned away from him, mourning her father's affair. She would not look at him except sideways, and would not speak to him except briefly. Then she asked him to make for her an image in his likeness, and he made it for her. She glorified it, prostrated to it, and her maidservants prostrated with her. It became an idol worshipped in his house, while he did not know of it until forty days had passed. The news spread among the Children of Israel, and Solomon learned of it, so he broke it, burned it, and then scattered it into the wind.

Fifth: what Mujahid related: Solomon said to Asif the devil, "How do you lead people astray?" The devil said to him, "Give me your ring so that I may tell you." So he gave him his ring, and the devil threw it into the sea until his kingdom was lost.

Sixth: what Abban related from Anas: "Solomon said one night, 'By God, I will certainly go round to my wives tonight, and they are a thousand women, each of whom will conceive a boy who will fight in the way of God,' and he did not add 'if God wills.'"

Anas said: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "By Him in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, had he said 'if God wills,' he would have had what he said. But none of them conceived that night except one woman, who bore him half a human."

﴿And We cast upon his throne a body﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions:

First: its meaning is "We placed a body in his kingdom," and the throne (kursi) is the kingdom.

Second: "We cast upon the seat of his kingdom a body."

Concerning this body there are four opinions:

First: it was Solomon's own body, which fell ill, so that his body lay upon his throne. This is related by Ibn Bahr.

Second: a son was born to him, and he feared for him, so he entrusted him to the clouds, where he was nourished, a day like a Friday, a Friday like a month, and a month like a year. He was not aware until the child fell dead upon his throne. This is related by al-Sha'bi.

Third: he had too much intercourse with his concubines (suriyyat, pl. of suriyya, a slave-concubine), seeking a child, so there was born to him half a human. He was the body that was placed upon his throne. This is related by al-Naqqash.

Fourth: God had placed Solomon's kingdom in his ring. Whenever he became junub (in a state of major ritual impurity) or went to relieve himself, he would take it off his hand and give it to the most trusted of his wives until he returned to take it back. Once he gave it to one of his wives and went to attend to his need. A devil came, took the form of Solomon before her, asked her for the ring, and she gave it to him. When Solomon came after him, he asked for it, and she said, "You have already taken it." Then Solomon realised what had happened.

There is disagreement about the name of this wife, with two opinions:

First: Jarada. This is related by Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr.

Second: al-Amina. This is related by Shahr ibn Hawshab.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib said: Solomon had placed his ring under his bed, and the devil took it from beneath him.

Mujahid said: Rather, the devil took it from his hand, because Solomon asked the devil, "How do you lead people astray?" The devil said, "Give me your ring so that I may tell you," and he gave him his ring. When the devil took the ring, he sat upon Solomon's throne, resembling him in appearance, entering upon his wives, judging without right and commanding what was not proper.

There is disagreement about whether he had intercourse with the women. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he used to come to them during their menstruation.

Mujahid said: he was prevented from coming to them, his kingdom was removed from him, and he went out fleeing to the seashore, seeking the hospitality of people and earning fish from fishermen for wages. When he told people that he was Solomon, they called him a liar. Meanwhile the devil sat on his throne. This is the meaning of His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And We cast upon his throne a body﴾.

There are four opinions about the name of this devil:

First: his name was Sakhr. This is related by Ibn 'Abbas.

Second: Asif. This is related by Mujahid.

Third: Haqiq. This is related by al-Suddi.

Fourth: Sayyid. This is related by Qatada.

Then, after the Children of Israel had disapproved of the devil's judgement, Solomon took back his fish from a fisherman. It is said that he had asked the fisherman for food, and Ibn 'Abbas said he took it as payment for carrying a fish that he had carried. When he split its belly, he found his ring inside it. This was forty days after his kingdom had been removed from him, which is the number of days during which the idol was worshipped in his house.

This is what Muqatil said. He reigned forty years: twenty years before the trial and twenty years after it.

The forty days during which he was removed from his kingdom were the month of Dhu al-Qa'da and ten days of Dhu al-Hijja. So the people prostrated to him when the ring returned to him and he regained his kingdom.

Yahya ibn Abi 'Amr al-Shaybani related that Solomon found his ring at Ascalon, and he walked from there to Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), in humility before God.

Ibn 'Abbas said: Then Solomon overcame the devil, placed him in a chest of marble, bound it with copper, and threw it into the sea.

This is the explanation of His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And We cast upon his throne a body﴾, ﴿then he turned in repentance﴾. Regarding this there are three interpretations:

First: then he returned to his kingdom. This is related by al-Dahhak.

Second: then he repented of his sin. This is related by Qatada.

Third: then he was cured of his illness. This is related by Ibn Bahr.

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿He said, "My Lord, forgive me and grant me a kingdom that will not befit anyone after me."﴾ Regarding this there are three opinions:

First: so that this would be a sign for him by which he would know God's pleasure and by which he would infer the acceptance of his repentance.

Second: so that he might be strengthened through it against those among the jinn who disobeyed him. The wind was then subjected to him.

Third: that no one after me during my lifetime should be able to take it from me, like the body that sat on my throne. This is related by al-Hasan.

﴿Indeed You are the Bestower﴾, that is, the Giver. Muqatil said: He asked God, Exalted is He, for a kingdom that would not befit anyone after him, after the trial. So God, Exalted is He, increased him with the wind and the devils after he had been tested. Al-Kalbi said: Solomon judged concerning the tilth when he was eleven years old, and he became king when he was twelve years old.

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿So We subjected the wind to him﴾, that is, We made it submissive to his obedience.

﴿running at his command﴾ admits two meanings:

First: it carries whatever he commands.

Second: it runs to wherever he commands it.

﴿gently﴾. Regarding this there are five interpretations:

First: good. This is related by Mujahid.

Second: swift. This is related by Qatada.

Third: obedient. This is related by al-Dahhak.

Fourth: soft. This is related by Ibn Zayd.

Fifth: neither a violent wind that causes harm nor a weak one that falls short. This is related by al-Hasan.

﴿wherever he willed﴾ (haythu asaba). Regarding this there are two meanings:

First: wherever he intended. This is related by Mujahid. Qatada said: it is in the dialect of Hajar.

Al-Asma'i said: the Arabs say "asaba al-sawab fa-akhta'a al-jawab" (he hit the right thing but erred in the answer), meaning he intended the right thing.

Second: wherever he aimed, taken from the arrow hitting the intended target.

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And the devils, every builder and diver﴾. That is, We subjected to him the devils: every builder, meaning on land, and every diver, meaning in the sea, to extract its ornaments and jewels.

﴿And others bound together in chains﴾. Regarding this there are three meanings:

First: in chains. This is related by Qatada.

Second: in shackles. This is related by al-Suddi.

Third: in bonds. This is related by Ibn 'Isa. The poet said:

They returned with plunder and captives, and we returned with kings bound in fetters.

Yahya ibn Salam said: He did not do this except because of their disbelief. When they believed, he released them and did not subject them.

And there was found on the wall of the city of Solomon, peace be upon him:

If a living being could attain eternity in its own time, Solomon son of Dawud would have attained it.
The spring of qitr (copper) flowed for him, abundant,
in it and from it a gift not to be counted.
After him none has remained in kingship, ascending,
until he was enclosed in a grave after a trench.
This teaches that kingship is cut off,
except from God, Lord of piety and of generosity.

First: what was mentioned earlier of the kingdom that would not befit anyone after him, through the subjection of the wind and the devils.

On this view, regarding His words ﴿so bestow or withhold without account﴾ there are two meanings:

First: bestow on whom you will among the jinn by releasing them, or withhold from whom you will among them from their labour, without any blame upon you for what you did to them. This is related by Qatada and al-Suddi.

Second: give to whom you will among people and withhold from whom you will among them.

﴿without account﴾ admits three meanings:

First: without measure in what you give and withhold. This is related by Ibn 'Isa.

Second: without hardship. This is related by Mujahid.

Third: without account that you will be held to on the Day of Resurrection. This is related by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

al-Hasan said: God has not bestowed any blessing upon anyone except that there is a consequence for him in it, except Solomon, for God, Exalted is He, says: ﴿This is Our gift, so bestow or withhold without account.﴾

Ibn Abi Najih related from Mujahid regarding His words ﴿This is Our gift﴾, the verse.

Solomon, peace be upon him, said: "We were given what people were given and what they were not given, and we knew what people knew and what they did not know. Yet we have not seen anything better than the fear of God in the unseen and the witnessed, moderation in wealth and poverty, and the word of truth in contentment and anger."

The second opinion: there is a transposition in the speech. Its implied sense is: "This is Our gift without account, so bestow or withhold." On this view, regarding "so bestow or withhold" there are two meanings:

First: without recompense.

Second: without scarcity.

The third opinion: this is a reference to an unmentioned hidden matter, which is what is related: that Solomon had in his loins the semen of a hundred men, and he had three hundred wives and seven hundred suriyyat. So God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿This is Our gift﴾, meaning the gift We have given you of the strength for intercourse, ﴿so bestow﴾ by having intercourse with whom you will of your wives, ﴿or withhold﴾ from having intercourse with whom you will of your wives.

On this view, regarding His words "without account" there are two meanings:

First: without being called to account for whom you had intercourse with or withdrew from.

Second: without a limited number of those whom you took or married.

This view is a departure from the apparent meaning towards claiming a hidden matter without evidence, but since it has been said, I have mentioned it.

First: he approached some of his wives during menstruation or something else. This is related by al-Hasan.

Love for her was cast upon him, while she turned away from him, mourning her father's affair. She would not look at him except sideways, and would not speak to him except briefly. First: Jarada. This is related by Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr.

Second: al-Amina. This is related by Shahr ibn Hawshab.

So God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿This is Our gift﴾, meaning the gift We have given you of the strength for intercourse, ﴿so bestow﴾ by having intercourse with whom you will of your wives, ﴿or withhold﴾ from having intercourse with whom you will of your wives.

On this view, regarding His words "without account" there are two meanings:

First: without being called to account for whom you had intercourse with or withdrew from.

Second: without a limited number of those whom you took or married.

This view is a departure from the apparent meaning towards claiming a hidden matter without evidence, but since it has been said, I have mentioned it.

﴿And We certainly tested Solomon﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations:

First: it means We tried him. This is related by al-Suddi.

Second: We punished him. This is related by al-Naqqash.

Concerning the trial by which he was punished, there are six opinions:

First: he approached some of his wives during menstruation or something else. This is related by al-Hasan.

Second: what Ibn 'Abbas related: he said, Solomon had a woman called Jarada. Her family had a dispute with a people, and they brought the matter before Solomon. He judged between them with the truth, but he wished that the right had been with her family. It was then said to him, "Affliction will befall you," and he kept wondering whether the affliction would come to him from the earth or from the sky.

Third: what Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib related: Solomon secluded himself from the people for three days, not judging between anyone and not granting justice to the wronged against the wrongdoer. So God Most High revealed to him: "I did not appoint you so that you would be hidden from My servants, but so that you would judge between them and grant justice to their wronged."

Fourth: what Shahr ibn Hawshab related: Solomon took captive the daughter of the king of Ghazzan on an island of the islands of the sea called Saydun. Love for her was cast upon him, while she turned away from him, mourning her father's affair. She would not look at him except sideways, and would not speak to him except briefly. Then she asked him to make for her an image in his likeness, and he made it for her. She glorified it, prostrated to it, and her maidservants prostrated with her. It became an idol worshipped in his house, while he did not know of it until forty days had passed. The news spread among the Children of Israel, and Solomon learned of it, so he broke it, burned it, and then scattered it into the wind.

Fifth: what Mujahid related: Solomon said to Asif the devil, "How do you lead people astray?" The devil said to him, "Give me your ring so that I may tell you." So he gave him his ring, and the devil threw it into the sea until his kingdom was lost.

Sixth: what Abban related from Anas: "Solomon said one night, 'By God, I will certainly go round to my wives tonight, and they are a thousand women, each of whom will conceive a boy who will fight in the way of God,' and he did not add 'if God wills.'"

Anas said: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "By Him in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, had he said 'if God wills,' he would have had what he said. But none of them conceived that night except one woman, who bore him half a human."

﴿And We cast upon his throne a body﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions:

First: its meaning is "We placed a body in his kingdom," and the throne (kursi) is the kingdom.

Second: "We cast upon the seat of his kingdom a body."

Concerning this body there are four opinions:

First: it was Solomon's own body, which fell ill, so that his body lay upon his throne. This is related by Ibn Bahr.

Second: a son was born to him, and he feared for him, so he entrusted him to the clouds, where he was nourished, a day like a Friday, a Friday like a month, and a month like a year. He was not aware until the child fell dead upon his throne. This is related by al-Sha'bi.

Third: he had too much intercourse with his concubines (suriyyat, pl. of suriyya, a slave-concubine), seeking a child, so there was born to him half a human. He was the body that was placed upon his throne. This is related by al-Naqqash.

Fourth: God had placed Solomon's kingdom in his ring. Whenever he became junub (in a state of major ritual impurity) or went to relieve himself, he would take it off his hand and give it to the most trusted of his wives until he returned to take it back. Once he gave it to one of his wives and went to attend to his need. A devil came, took the form of Solomon before her, asked her for the ring, and she gave it to him. When Solomon came after him, he asked for it, and she said, "You have already taken it." Then Solomon realised what had happened.

There is disagreement about the name of this wife, with two opinions:

First: Jarada. This is related by Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr.

Second: al-Amina. This is related by Shahr ibn Hawshab.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib said: Solomon had placed his ring under his bed, and the devil took it from beneath him.

Mujahid said: Rather, the devil took it from his hand, because Solomon asked the devil, "How do you lead people astray?" The devil said, "Give me your ring so that I may tell you," and he gave him his ring. When the devil took the ring, he sat upon Solomon's throne, resembling him in appearance, entering upon his wives, judging without right and commanding what was not proper.

There is disagreement about whether he had intercourse with the women. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he used to come to them during their menstruation.

Mujahid said: he was prevented from coming to them, his kingdom was removed from him, and he went out fleeing to the seashore, seeking the hospitality of people and earning fish from fishermen for wages. When he told people that he was Solomon, they called him a liar. Meanwhile the devil sat on his throne. This is the meaning of His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And We cast upon his throne a body﴾.

There are four opinions about the name of this devil:

First: his name was Sakhr. This is related by Ibn 'Abbas.

Second: Asif. This is related by Mujahid.

Third: Haqiq. This is related by al-Suddi.

Fourth: Sayyid. This is related by Qatada.

Then, after the Children of Israel had disapproved of the devil's judgement, Solomon took back his fish from a fisherman. It is said that he had asked the fisherman for food, and Ibn 'Abbas said he took it as payment for carrying a fish that he had carried. When he split its belly, he found his ring inside it. This was forty days after his kingdom had been removed from him, which is the number of days during which the idol was worshipped in his house.

This is what Muqatil said. He reigned forty years: twenty years before the trial and twenty years after it.

The forty days during which he was removed from his kingdom were the month of Dhu al-Qa'da and ten days of Dhu al-Hijja. So the people prostrated to him when the ring returned to him and he regained his kingdom.

Yahya ibn Abi 'Amr al-Shaybani related that Solomon found his ring at Ascalon, and he walked from there to Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), in humility before God.

Ibn 'Abbas said: Then Solomon overcame the devil, placed him in a chest of marble, bound it with copper, and threw it into the sea.

This is the explanation of His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And We cast upon his throne a body﴾, ﴿then he turned in repentance﴾. Regarding this there are three interpretations:

First: then he returned to his kingdom. This is related by al-Dahhak.

Second: then he repented of his sin. This is related by Qatada.

Third: then he was cured of his illness. This is related by Ibn Bahr.

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿He said, "My Lord, forgive me and grant me a kingdom that will not befit anyone after me."﴾ Regarding this there are three opinions:

First: so that this would be a sign for him by which he would know God's pleasure and by which he would infer the acceptance of his repentance.

Second: so that he might be strengthened through it against those among the jinn who disobeyed him. The wind was then subjected to him.

Third: that no one after me during my lifetime should be able to take it from me, like the body that sat on my throne. This is related by al-Hasan.

﴿Indeed You are the Bestower﴾, that is, the Giver. Muqatil said: He asked God, Exalted is He, for a kingdom that would not befit anyone after him, after the trial. So God, Exalted is He, increased him with the wind and the devils after he had been tested. Al-Kalbi said: Solomon judged concerning the tilth when he was eleven years old, and he became king when he was twelve years old.

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿So We subjected the wind to him﴾, that is, We made it submissive to his obedience.

﴿running at his command﴾ admits two meanings:

First: it carries whatever he commands.

Second: it runs to wherever he commands it.

﴿gently﴾. Regarding this there are five interpretations:

First: good. This is related by Mujahid.

Second: swift. This is related by Qatada.

Third: obedient. This is related by al-Dahhak.

Fourth: soft. This is related by Ibn Zayd.

Fifth: neither a violent wind that causes harm nor a weak one that falls short. This is related by al-Hasan.

﴿wherever he willed﴾ (haythu asaba). Regarding this there are two meanings:

First: wherever he intended. This is related by Mujahid. Qatada said: it is in the dialect of Hajar.

Al-Asma'i said: the Arabs say "asaba al-sawab fa-akhta'a al-jawab" (he hit the right thing but erred in the answer), meaning he intended the right thing.

Second: wherever he aimed, taken from the arrow hitting the intended target.

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And the devils, every builder and diver﴾. That is, We subjected to him the devils: every builder, meaning on land, and every diver, meaning in the sea, to extract its ornaments and jewels.

﴿And others bound together in chains﴾. Regarding this there are three meanings:

First: in chains. This is related by Qatada.

Second: in shackles. This is related by al-Suddi.

Third: in bonds. This is related by Ibn 'Isa. The poet said:

They returned with plunder and captives, and we returned with kings bound in fetters.

Yahya ibn Salam said: He did not do this except because of their disbelief. When they believed, he released them and did not subject them.

And there was found on the wall of the city of Solomon, peace be upon him:

If a living being could attain eternity in its own time, Solomon son of Dawud would have attained it.
The spring of qitr (copper) flowed for him, abundant,
in it and from it a gift not to be counted.
After him none has remained in kingship, ascending,
until he was enclosed in a grave after a trench.
This teaches that kingship is cut off,
except from God, Lord of piety and of generosity.

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿This is Our gift﴾. Regarding what is indicated by "this" there are three opinions:

First: what was mentioned earlier of the kingdom that would not befit anyone after him, through the subjection of the wind and the devils.

On this view, regarding His words ﴿so bestow or withhold without account﴾ there are two meanings:

First: bestow on whom you will among the jinn by releasing them, or withhold from whom you will among them from their labour, without any blame upon you for what you did to them. This is related by Qatada and al-Suddi.

Second: give to whom you will among people and withhold from whom you will among them.

﴿without account﴾ admits three meanings:

First: without measure in what you give and withhold. This is related by Ibn 'Isa.

Second: without hardship. This is related by Mujahid.

Third: without account that you will be held to on the Day of Resurrection. This is related by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

al-Hasan said: God has not bestowed any blessing upon anyone except that there is a consequence for him in it, except Solomon, for God, Exalted is He, says: ﴿This is Our gift, so bestow or withhold without account.﴾

Ibn Abi Najih related from Mujahid regarding His words ﴿This is Our gift﴾, the verse.

Solomon, peace be upon him, said: "We were given what people were given and what they were not given, and we knew what people knew and what they did not know. Yet we have not seen anything better than the fear of God in the unseen and the witnessed, moderation in wealth and poverty, and the word of truth in contentment and anger."

The second opinion: there is a transposition in the speech. Its implied sense is: "This is Our gift without account, so bestow or withhold." On this view, regarding "so bestow or withhold" there are two meanings:

First: without recompense.

Second: without scarcity.

The third opinion: this is a reference to an unmentioned hidden matter, which is what is related: that Solomon had in his loins the semen of a hundred men, and he had three hundred wives and seven hundred suriyyat. So God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿This is Our gift﴾, meaning the gift We have given you of the strength for intercourse, ﴿so bestow﴾ by having intercourse with whom you will of your wives, ﴿or withhold﴾ from having intercourse with whom you will of your wives.

On this view, regarding His words "without account" there are two meanings:

First: without being called to account for whom you had intercourse with or withdrew from.

Second: without a limited number of those whom you took or married.

This view is a departure from the apparent meaning towards claiming a hidden matter without evidence, but since it has been said, I have mentioned it.

﴿And remember Our servant Job, when he called upon his Lord: "Indeed, Satan has touched me with fatigue and torment."﴾ It is said he was Ayyub ibn Hawṣ ibn Ruʿawīl, and that he lived in the time of Yaʿqub ibn Ishaq. He married Yaʿqub's daughter, Ilya bint Yaʿqub. His mother was the daughter of Lut (peace be upon him), and his father Hawṣ was among those who believed in Ibrahim (peace be upon him).

Regarding His words ﴿Satan has touched me﴾, there are two interpretations:

First: The "touch" of Satan means his whispering and his reminding him of the blessings he once had and of the trial he had come to. This is related by Ibn ʿIsa.

Second: Satan asked Allah, Exalted is He, for permission to afflict him in his wealth, and He permitted him. Then (he asked to afflict him) in his family and his home, and He permitted him. Then in his body, and He permitted him. Then (he asked to afflict) his heart, but He did not permit him. Ibn ʿAbbas said: this is His words ﴿Satan has touched me﴾, and so on.

﴿with fatigue and torment﴾: Regarding this there are three interpretations:

First: By "fatigue" is meant pain, and by "torment" is meant sickness. This was said by Mubashshir ibn ʿUbayd.

Second: The "fatigue" was in his body, and the "torment" was in his wealth. This was said by al-Suddi.

Third: "Nusb" means hardship, and "ʿadhab" means affliction.

(p-102) His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Strike with your foot; this is a cool bath and a drink﴾. Qatadah said: "They are two springs in the land of Syria, in a place called al-Jabiyah."

Regarding these two there are two opinions:

First: He bathed in one of them, and Allah removed the outward part of his illness; and he drank from the other, and Allah removed the inward part of his illness. This was said by al-Hasan.

Second: He bathed in one of them and was healed, and he drank from the other and was satisfied. This was said by Qatadah.

Regarding "the bath" (al-mughtasal) there are two interpretations:

First: It was the place where he bathed. This was said by Muqatil.

Second: It is the water with which he bathed. This was said by Ibn Qutaybah.

Regarding the duration of his illness there are two opinions:

First: Seven years and seven months. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Second: Eighteen years, related by Anas as a marfuʿ (traced back to the Prophet, ﷺ) report.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And We gave him his family and the like of them with them﴾. Regarding what befell them there are three sayings:

First: They had been ill, and Allah cured them.

Second: They had been absent from him, and Allah returned them to him. These two sayings were related by Ibn Bahr.

Third, which is the view of the majority: they had died.

Based on this, regarding His giving them to him and the like of them with them, there are five sayings:

First: Allah returned to him his family, his children and his livestock in their own persons, because He had caused them to die before their appointed times as a trial, and He granted him the like of them from their offspring. This was said by al-Hasan.

Second: Allah, Glorified is He, returned them to him in their own persons and granted him the like of them from others. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Third: He returned to him their reward in Paradise and granted him the like of them in this world. This was said by al-Suddi.

Fourth: He returned to him his family in Paradise, and he had relations with his wife, and she brought him the like of them in this world.

Fifth: He did not return to him any of them after their death, and they had been thirteen sons. Allah granted him from his wife, who was the mother of the one who had died, the like of them (p-103), and she bore him twenty-six sons. This was said by al-Dahhak.

﴿Mercy from Us﴾: that is, a blessing from Us.

﴿And a reminder for those of understanding﴾: that is, a lesson for those possessed of intellect.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And take in your hand a bundle (ḍighth) and strike with it, and do not break your oath﴾. Ayyub had sworn, during his illness, that he would strike his wife one hundred lashes.

Regarding the cause of this there are three sayings:

First: What Ibn ʿAbbas said: Iblis met her in the form of a physician, and she asked him to treat Ayyub. He said, "I will treat him on condition that when he is cured he says, 'You have cured me,' and I want no reward other than that." She said yes. So she suggested this to Ayyub, and he swore that he would strike her.

Second: What Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib related: she brought him more bread than she usually brought, and he feared that she had stolen it, so he swore that he would strike her.

Third: What Yahya ibn Salam related: Satan tempted her to get Ayyub to slaughter a young goat so that he might be cured by it. So he swore that he would flog her. When Ayyub was cured, and Allah, Exalted is He, knew of his wife's faith, He commanded him, out of gentleness toward her and kindness to him, to take in his hand a bundle (ḍighth).

Regarding the word ḍighth there are seven sayings:

First: It is a bundle of palm fronds gathered together by their stalks. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Second: Al-athl (tamarisk). This was related by Mujahid, and Mujahid also said it.

Third: Ears of grain (al-sunbul). This was related by Yahya ibn Salam.

Fourth: Dry grass (al-thumam al-yabis). This was said by Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib.

Fifth: Moist trees. This was said by al-Akhfash.

Sixth: A bundle of grass. This was said by Qutrub, who recited the verse of al-Kumayt:

She shies away from a stallion, when the herdsman points to her with a bundle of grass.

Seventh: A handful of straw, or grass, or palm stalks. This was said by Abu ʿUbayda.

(p-104) ﴿Strike﴾: strike with the number of strokes you swore, which is that he should gather one hundred from the count of the bundle and strike her with it in a single blow, in which he is certain that all of them reach her body; this takes the place of one hundred separate lashes.

﴿And do not break your oath﴾: that is, regarding the oath. Regarding this there are two sayings:

First: That this is specific to Ayyub, said by Mujahid.

Second: It is general to Ayyub and others of this nation, said by Qatadah.

Our own view on this, as a school of thought, is: if this concerns a prescribed punishment (hadd) of Allah, Exalted is He, it is permitted for one excused by illness or infirmity, and not permitted for anyone else. If it concerns an oath, it is permitted for the one excused and for others when the pain of the one struck accompanies it. If it is free of pain, then regarding whether he fulfils the oath there are two views:

First: He fulfils it, because the number sworn upon exists.

Second: He does not fulfil it, because the intended pain is absent.

﴿Indeed, We found him patient﴾: this may bear two meanings: First: patient in obedience. Second: patient in trial.

﴿An excellent servant﴾: that is, an excellent servant in his patience.

﴿Indeed, he was one who often turned back (to his Lord)﴾: that is, turning back to his Lord.

Regarding his trial there are two sayings:

First: It was a trial of testing and a degree of reward, not on account of a sin for which he was punished.

Second: It was on account of a sin for which he was punished by this trial. Regarding this there are two sayings:

First: He entered upon one of the tyrants, saw an evil, and remained silent about it.

Second: He slaughtered a sheep and ate it while his neighbour was hungry and he did not feed him.

First: The "touch" of Satan means his whispering and his reminding him of the blessings he once had and of the trial he had come to. This is related by Ibn ʿIsa.

Second: Satan asked Allah, Exalted is He, for permission to afflict him in his wealth, and He permitted him. Then (he asked to afflict him) in his family and his home, and He permitted him.
