﴿with fatigue and torment﴾: Regarding this there are three interpretations:

First: By "fatigue" is meant pain, and by "torment" is meant sickness. This was said by Mubashshir ibn ʿUbayd.

Second: The "fatigue" was in his body, and the "torment" was in his wealth. This was said by al-Suddi.

Third: "Nusb" means hardship, and "ʿadhab" means affliction.

(p-102) His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Strike with your foot; this is a cool bath and a drink﴾. Qatadah said: "They are two springs in the land of Syria, in a place called al-Jabiyah."

Regarding these two there are two opinions:

First: He bathed in one of them, and Allah removed the outward part of his illness; and he drank from the other, and Allah removed the inward part of his illness. This was said by al-Hasan.

Second: He bathed in one of them and was healed, and he drank from the other and was satisfied. This was said by Qatadah.

Regarding "the bath" (al-mughtasal) there are two interpretations:

First: It was the place where he bathed. This was said by Muqatil.

Second: It is the water with which he bathed. This was said by Ibn Qutaybah.

Regarding the duration of his illness there are two opinions:

First: Seven years and seven months. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Second: Eighteen years, related by Anas as a marfuʿ (traced back to the Prophet, ﷺ) report.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And We gave him his family and the like of them with them﴾. Regarding what befell them there are three sayings:

First: They had been ill, and Allah cured them.

Second: They had been absent from him, and Allah returned them to him. These two sayings were related by Ibn Bahr.

Third, which is the view of the majority: they had died.

Based on this, regarding His giving them to him and the like of them with them, there are five sayings:

First: Allah returned to him his family, his children and his livestock in their own persons, because He had caused them to die before their appointed times as a trial, and He granted him the like of them from their offspring. This was said by al-Hasan.

Second: Allah, Glorified is He, returned them to him in their own persons and granted him the like of them from others. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Third: He returned to him their reward in Paradise and granted him the like of them in this world. This was said by al-Suddi.

Fourth: He returned to him his family in Paradise, and he had relations with his wife, and she brought him the like of them in this world.

Fifth: He did not return to him any of them after their death, and they had been thirteen sons. Allah granted him from his wife, who was the mother of the one who had died, the like of them (p-103), and she bore him twenty-six sons. This was said by al-Dahhak.

﴿Mercy from Us﴾: that is, a blessing from Us.

﴿And a reminder for those of understanding﴾: that is, a lesson for those possessed of intellect.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And take in your hand a bundle (ḍighth) and strike with it, and do not break your oath﴾. Ayyub had sworn, during his illness, that he would strike his wife one hundred lashes.

Regarding the cause of this there are three sayings:

First: What Ibn ʿAbbas said: Iblis met her in the form of a physician, and she asked him to treat Ayyub. He said, "I will treat him on condition that when he is cured he says, 'You have cured me,' and I want no reward other than that." She said yes. So she suggested this to Ayyub, and he swore that he would strike her.

Second: What Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib related: she brought him more bread than she usually brought, and he feared that she had stolen it, so he swore that he would strike her.

Third: What Yahya ibn Salam related: Satan tempted her to get Ayyub to slaughter a young goat so that he might be cured by it. So he swore that he would flog her. When Ayyub was cured, and Allah, Exalted is He, knew of his wife's faith, He commanded him, out of gentleness toward her and kindness to him, to take in his hand a bundle (ḍighth).

Regarding the word ḍighth there are seven sayings:

First: It is a bundle of palm fronds gathered together by their stalks. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Second: Al-athl (tamarisk). This was related by Mujahid, and Mujahid also said it.

Third: Ears of grain (al-sunbul). This was related by Yahya ibn Salam.

Fourth: Dry grass (al-thumam al-yabis). This was said by Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib.

Fifth: Moist trees. This was said by al-Akhfash.

Sixth: A bundle of grass. This was said by Qutrub, who recited the verse of al-Kumayt:

She shies away from a stallion, when the herdsman points to her with a bundle of grass.

Seventh: A handful of straw, or grass, or palm stalks. This was said by Abu ʿUbayda.

﴿And do not break your oath﴾: that is, regarding the oath. Regarding this there are two sayings:

First: That this is specific to Ayyub, said by Mujahid.

Second: It is general to Ayyub and others of this nation, said by Qatadah.

If it concerns an oath, it is permitted for the one excused and for others when the pain of the one struck accompanies it. If it is free of pain, then regarding whether he fulfils the oath there are two views:

First: He fulfils it, because the number sworn upon exists.

Second: He does not fulfil it, because the intended pain is absent.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-‘Uyun) on Surah 38, verses 45–48:**

First: the *al-aydi* (الأيْدِي, "the hands") means strength in worship, and *al-absar* (الأبْصارَ, "the insights") means understanding of the religion. This is the view of Ibn ‘Abbas.

Second: *al-aydi* means strength in carrying out God's command, and *al-absar* means knowledge of the Book of God. This is the view of Qatadah.

Third: *al-aydi* means blessing. This was transmitted by al-Dahhak. *Al-absar* means intellects. This is the view of Mujahid.

Fourth: *al-aydi* means physical strength in their bodies, and *al-absar* means strength in their religion. This is the view of ‘Atiyyah.

Fifth: *al-aydi* means action, and *al-absar* means knowledge. This is the view of Ibn Bahr.

Muqatil said: God mentioned Ibrahim, Ishaq and Ya‘qub, and did not mention Isma‘il along with them, because Ibrahim endured being thrown into the fire, Ishaq endured being sacrificed, and Ya‘qub endured the loss of his sight. Isma‘il was not tested with a trial.

God, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Indeed, We made them pure with a pure quality: the remembrance of the Abode﴾. On this there are five interpretations:

First: God removed from their hearts the world and its remembrance, and purified them with love of the Hereafter and its remembrance. This is the view of Malik ibn Dinar.

Second: We chose them for the best of what is in the Hereafter and gave it to them. This is the view of Ibn Ziyad.

Third: We purified them with the pure essence of the revealed Books, in which is the remembrance of the Abode of the Hereafter. This is a view that has been transmitted (ma’thur).

Fourth: We purified them with prophethood and the remembrance of the Abode of the Hereafter. This is the view of Muqatil.

Fifth: We purified them from defects and afflictions, and made them remember the Abode of the Hereafter. This was related by al-Naqqash.

﴿أتْرابٌ﴾ (atrab) has five interpretations:

First: peers of the same age (aqran), said by 'Ata'.

Second: likenesses (amthal), said by Mujahid.

Third: companions who are affectionate toward one another, neither hating one another nor being jealous of one another, related by 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Hatim.

Fourth: of equal ages, daughters of thirty-three years, said by Yahya ibn Salam.

Fifth: of the same age as their husbands, in that He created them according to their measures. Ibn 'Isa said: al-turab (التُّرْب) is al-lidah (الِّدَة, equals in age), and it is derived from playing with dust (al-la'ib bi al-turab).

﴿This! Let them taste it: boiling water and ghassaq.﴾ That is, from it there is boiling water, and from it there is ghassaq. Ḥamīm means something hot. There are six views concerning ghassaq:

The first: it is the bitter cold (zamharīr, extreme cold). This was said by Ibn ʿAbbās. So they are punished with the heat and the cold of the earth.

The second: it is the pus that flows from their skins. This was said by ʿAṭiyya.

The third: it is their tears that flow from their eyes. This was said by Qatāda.

The fourth: it is a spring in Hell into which flows the venom of every venomous creature, whether a snake or a scorpion. This was said by Kaʿb al-Aḥbār.

(p-107) The fifth: it is the stench. Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī related it as a marfūʿ (attributed to the Prophet ﷺ).

The sixth: it is blackness and darkness, which is the opposite of what is intended by the clarity and thinness of a drink. This was said by Ibn Baḥr.

Al-Marḥab and al-Ruḥb mean spaciousness, and from it the courtyard (al-raḥba) was named for its spaciousness. Its meaning is: may your places not be spacious for you. Al-Akhfash recited the words of Abū al-Aswad:

"When you come to a doorkeeper, he says 'Welcome!' (marḥaban), welcome to your valley, unconstricted."

(p-109) ﴿And they say: "What is the matter with us that we do not see men..."﴾ Mujāhid said: this is said by Abū Jahl and his followers in the Fire: "What is the matter with us that we do not see men whom we used to count among the wicked in the world? We do not see ʿAmmār, Khabbāb, Ṣuhayb and Bilāl."

﴿Did we take them in mockery?﴾ Mujāhid said: we took them in mockery in the world, and we were mistaken.

﴿Or have our eyes failed to see them?﴾ So we do not know where they are.

Al-Ḥasan said: all of that they did. They took them in mockery, and their eyes turned away from them, belittling them.

Abū ʿUbayda said: whoever read "sikhriyyan" with a kasra made it from mockery (al-huzʾ), and whoever read it with a ḍamma made it from subjugation (al-taskhīr). ﴿Or have our eyes failed to see them?﴾ That is: are they with us in the Fire, or have our eyes failed, so that we do not see them even though they are with us?

﴿This! Let them taste it: boiling water and ghassaq.﴾ That is, from it there is boiling water, and from it there is ghassaq. Ḥamīm means something hot. There are six views concerning ghassaq:

The first: it is the bitter cold (zamharīr, extreme cold). This was said by Ibn ʿAbbās. So they are punished with the heat and the cold of the earth.

The second: it is the pus that flows from their skins. This was said by ʿAṭiyya.

The third: it is their tears that flow from their eyes. This was said by Qatāda.

The fourth: it is a spring in Hell into which flows the venom of every venomous creature, whether a snake or a scorpion. This was said by Kaʿb al-Aḥbār.

(p-107) The fifth: it is the stench. Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī related it as a marfūʿ (attributed to the Prophet ﷺ).

The sixth: it is blackness and darkness, which is the opposite of what is intended by the clarity and thinness of a drink. This was said by Ibn Baḥr.

Regarding this name there are two views:

The first: al-Naqqāsh reported that it is in the language of the Turks.

The second: Ibn Baḥr and Ibn ʿĪsā reported that it is Arabic and derived. Its derivation has been disputed in two ways:

The first: it is from al-ghasaq, which is darkness. This was said by Ibn Baḥr.

The second: it is from ghasaqat al-qarḥa, "the wound discharged" (taghsiqu ghasaqan), when it flows. Quṭrub recited the words of a poet:

"The eye is struck for their separation, it flows in the strangeness of its secret."

Ibn ʿĪsā followed this view.

In "ghassāq" there are two readings, with light and with heavy emphasis (tashdīd), and regarding them there are two views:

The first: they are two dialects with one meaning. This was said by al-Akhfash.

The second: their meanings differ. The light form refers to the noun, and the heavy form refers to the verb. It was also said that there is an inversion (taqdīm wa ta'khīr) in the speech, and its intended sense is: "This is boiling water, and this is ghassaq, so let them taste it."

﴿And other punishments of its kind, in pairs.﴾ Concerning this there are three views:

The first: and other kinds of punishment of its type. This was said by al-Suddī.

The second: and other kinds of the punishment of this world, which exist in the Hereafter but were not seen in this world. This was said by al-Ḥasan.

The third: it is the zamharīr (bitter cold). This was said by Ibn Masʿūd.

Concerning "pairs" (azwāj) here there are three views:

The first: kinds.

The second: colours.

The third: gathered together.

(p-108) ﴿This is a troop rushing in with you.﴾ A troop after a troop, that is, a people after a people, rushing into the Fire, that is, entering it.

Concerning "troop" there are two views:

The first: they are the sons of Iblīs.

The second: they are the sons of Ādam. This was said by al-Ḥasan.

The second view is that both troops are the sons of Ādam, except that the first are the leaders and the second are the followers.

Al-Naqqāsh reported that the first troop are the leaders of the polytheists and their feeders on the Day of Badr, and the second troop are their followers at Badr.

Concerning the speaker of ﴿This is a troop rushing in with you﴾ there are two views:

The first: the angels said to the sons of Iblīs, when they went ahead into the Fire: "This is a troop rushing in with you," indicating the sons of Ādam when they entered it.

The sons of Iblīs said: ﴿No welcome to them! They are going to burn in the Fire.﴾ ﴿They said﴾, that is, the sons of Ādam: ﴿Rather, no welcome to you! You brought this upon us, so what an evil resting place!﴾

The second view: when God commanded the second troop to enter, God said to the first troop: ﴿This is a troop rushing in with you﴾, and they answered Him: ﴿No welcome to them! They are going to burn in the Fire.﴾ Then the second troop answered them: ﴿Rather, no welcome to you! You brought it upon us.﴾ Concerning this there are three views:

The first: its meaning is: you established it for us and made for us a precedent (qadam) through it. This was said by al-Kalbī.

The second: you brought this punishment upon us in the Fire by leading us astray from guidance. This was said by al-Ḍaḥḥāk. ﴿So what an evil resting place!﴾, that is, what an evil abode is the Fire.

The third: you brought upon us the disbelief for which we deserved this punishment in the Fire. This was reported by Ibn Ziyād.

﴿They say: "Our Lord, whoever brought this upon us, add to him double punishment in the Fire."﴾ The verse may have two meanings:

The first: the first troop said it in answer to the second troop.

The second: the troop said it following their first statement, confirming what they said when they were denying.

Concerning the interpretation of ﴿whoever brought this upon us﴾ there are two views:

The first: whoever instituted and established it. This was said by al-Kalbī.

The second: whoever adorned it. This was said by Muqātil.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: It is a momentous news﴾. Concerning it there are two opinions:

One of them is that it is the Resurrection, because God Most High has informed us of it in His Books.

The second opinion is that it is the Qur'an. This was said by Mujahid, al-Dahhak and al-Suddi.

﴿You are turning away from it﴾. Al-Dahhak said: "You are denying it."

Al-Suddi said: "He means by it the polytheists."

Regarding calling it a "news," there are two explanations:

One: because God informed us of it, and so we came to know it.

The second: because it contains the news of the earlier peoples.

Regarding describing it as "momentous," there are two explanations:

One: because of the greatness of its status and the abundance of its benefit.

The second: because of the greatness of what it contains of warnings and commands.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿I had no knowledge of the Exalted Assembly﴾. Ibn Abbas said: "It means the angels."

﴿when they dispute﴾. Concerning it there are two explanations:

One: it refers to His saying to the angels: ﴿Indeed, I am going to place upon the earth a successor﴾, up to ﴿They said: Will You place therein one who causes corruption...﴾ and the rest of the verse. This is the dispute, as said by Ibn Abbas.

I said, 'Walking on foot to the congregations, perfecting the ablution in the harsh cold, and waiting in the mosques for one prayer after another.' He said, 'And what are the degrees?' Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 38, verses 71–88:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying: ﴿O Iblis, what prevented you from prostrating to that which I created with My two hands?﴾ Regarding this there are three interpretations:

The first: "With My power." This was said by Ali ibn Asim.

The second: "With My might (qudra)." From this is the saying of the poet:

؎ I have borne from Afra what is not mine to bear, nor could the towering mountains bear it, nor do they have two hands.

The third: "Because I undertook its creation Myself." This was said by Ibn Isa.

﴿Have you become arrogant⁠﴾, meaning, against obedience, or did you deem yourself too exalted to prostrate?

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying: ﴿He said, "So the truth, and the truth I say"﴾. Regarding this there are three interpretations:

The first: "I am the Truth, and I say the truth." This was said by Mujahid.

The second: "The truth is from Me, and the truth is My word." Narrated by al-Hakam.

(p-112) The third: its meaning is "Truly, I will fill Hell with you and those among mankind who follow you, all together." This was said by al-Hasan.

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying: ﴿Say, "I do not ask you for any wage for it"﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations:

The first: "Say, O Muhammad, to the polytheists: I do not ask you for any reward for what I call you to of obedience to Allah." This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: "I do not ask you for any reward for what I have brought you of the Qur'an." This was said by Ata.

﴿And I am not of those who pretend⁠﴾. Regarding this there are three interpretations:

The first: "And I am not of those who presume (to speak) for this Qur'an from my own self."

The second: "And I am not of those who presume to command you with what I have not been commanded."

The third: "And I am not one who burdens you with a wage." This is the meaning of the saying of Muqatil.

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying: ﴿And you will surely know its news after a time⁠﴾. Regarding this there are three interpretations: The first: the news of the Qur'an, that it is true.

The second: the news of Muhammad (ﷺ), that he is a Messenger.

The third: the news of the threat, that it is true.

﴿After a time⁠﴾. Regarding this there are three interpretations:

The first: after death. This was said by Qatadah.

Al-Hasan said: "O son of Adam, at death the certain news comes to you."

The second: the Day of Badr. This was said by al-Suddi.

The third: the Day of Resurrection. This was said by Ibn Zayd and Ikrimah, and Allah knows best.

The second: "With My might (qudra)." From this is the saying of the poet:

؎ I have borne from Afra what is not mine to bear, nor could the towering mountains bear it, nor do they have two hands.

The third: "Because I undertook its creation Myself." This was said by Ibn Isa.

The first: "I am the Truth, and I say the truth." This was said by Mujahid.

The first: "Say, O Muhammad, to the polytheists: I do not ask you for any reward for what I call you to of obedience to Allah." This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: "I do not ask you for any reward for what I have brought you of the Qur'an." This was said by Ata.

The first: "And I am not of those who presume (to speak) for this Qur'an from my own self."

The second: "And I am not of those who presume to command you with what I have not been commanded."

The third: "And I am not one who burdens you with a wage." This is the meaning of the saying of Muqatil.

The second: the news of Muhammad (ﷺ), that he is a Messenger.

The third: the news of the threat, that it is true.
